    report: # Cold Regions Science and Technology (CRST): current author requirements

**Journal:** *Cold Regions Science and Technology* (Elsevier; print ISSN 0165-232X, online ISSN 1872-7441)  
**Accessed:** 24 September 2026 (UTC)  
**Scope of review:** Current official Elsevier/ScienceDirect material only. **[E]** = explicit rule or statement in an official source; **[I]** = inference/operational recommendation, clearly identified.

## Primary official sources

1. **“Guide for authors - Cold Regions Science and Technology - ISSN 0165-232X | ScienceDirect.com by Elsevier”**  
   https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/cold-regions-science-and-technology/publish/guide-for-authors
2. **“Generative AI policies for journals”**  
   https://www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/generative-ai-policies-for-journals
3. **“What should be included in a cover letter? | Journal Article Publishing Support Center”** (last updated 18 May 2026)  
   https://www.elsevier.support/publishing/answer/what-should-be-included-in-a-cover-letter

## Verified requirements

### 1. Aims and scope

- **[E]** CRST covers scientific and technical problems of cold environments in polar and temperate locations, including fundamental cryospheric science with cold-regions applications and engineering topics related to the cryosphere.
- **[E]** Its emphasized subjects are the physical and mechanical aspects of ice (including glaciers and sea ice), snow and avalanches, ice–water systems, ice-bonded soils, and permafrost. Earth science, materials science, offshore and river-ice engineering, icing of ships/structures, trafficability, and cold-regions technological advances are also in scope.
- **[E]** Theoretical papers must include “a detailed discussion of the potential application of the theory to address cold regions problems.”
- **[I]** A roof-snow-management paper is facially within the stated “snow and snow avalanche” and applied cold-regions engineering scope, but actual suitability remains an editorial decision.

### 2. Article types and review

- **[E]** Permitted regular article types are **Research Articles, Review Articles, and Short Communications**.
- **[E]** The journal uses **single-anonymized review**; suitable papers are typically assessed by at least two independent reviewers.
- **[I]** The current CRST Guide does not state body-word, page, figure-count, table-count, or reference-count limits for these article types. This is an absence in the current published Guide, not an affirmative guarantee that Editorial Manager will impose no field/file limits.

### 3. Manuscript preparation

- **[E] Source files:** Submit editable files for the entire submission. Word must be `.doc`/`.docx`; LaTeX must be `.tex`. A PDF is **not** an acceptable source file. Word manuscripts must use a single-column layout; double-column layout is permitted only for LaTeX.
- **[E] Title page:** Include a concise informative title; author names in submission-system order; full affiliations and postal addresses with country; one clearly identified corresponding author and email; and present/permanent-address footnotes where applicable.
- **[E] Abstract:** Concise and factual, **maximum 250 words**; state purpose, basic procedures, main findings (including statistical significance where applicable), principal conclusions, and novel/important aspects. It must stand alone; avoid references and undefined nonstandard abbreviations.
- **[E] Keywords:** **1–7**, in English; avoid multiword terms where possible and use abbreviations only if established.
- **[E] Highlights:** **Required** at submission as a **separate editable file**, with “highlights” in the filename; **3–5 bullets**, each no more than **85 characters including spaces**.
- **[E] Graphical abstract:** Encouraged, not stated as mandatory. Upload separately; image should be **531 × 1328 pixels (h × w) or proportionally larger**, readable at 5 × 13 cm; preferred formats: TIFF, EPS, PDF, or MS Office.
- **[E] Structure:** Divide the manuscript into clearly defined sections. Put acknowledgements in a separate section immediately before the references, not on the title page or in a footnote.
- **[E] CRediT:** The corresponding author is required to report co-author contributions using the CRediT taxonomy.
- **[E] Line numbering:** The submission checklist requires **continuous line numbers throughout the manuscript, from title through the end of figure/table captions**.

### 4. Tables, figures, and supplementary files

- **[E] Tables:** Submit as editable text, not images. They may be placed beside the relevant text or on separate pages at the end. Cite all tables; number in order of appearance; supply captions and notes; avoid vertical rules and cell shading.
- **[E] Figures/artwork:** Supply figures and other artwork as **separate files** with logical names such as `Figure_1`; cite and number them in order. Text graphics may be embedded in the manuscript. Every artwork item needs a caption with a brief title and description, explaining symbols/abbreviations.
- **[E] Artwork formats/resolution:**
  - Vector drawings: EPS or PDF; embed fonts or save text as graphics.
  - Photographs: TIFF/JPG/PNG, minimum **300 dpi**; minimum width 1063 px (single column) or 2244 px (full page).
  - Bitmapped line drawings: TIFF/JPG/PNG, minimum **1000 dpi**; minimum width 3543 px (single column) or 7480 px (full page).
  - Charts/large or shaded tables: XLS/XLSX, clearly readable.
  - Annotated images: PPT/PPTX; legible text; embedded images minimum 300 dpi.
- **[E]** Do not submit low-resolution artwork, disproportionately small labels, or combined multi-image/graph files unless comparison requires the combination.
- **[E] Supplementary material:** Cite it in the manuscript and submit it with the initial manuscript. Supply a concise caption for each file. It is published as received and is not production-edited; after initial submission it may be added/replaced only at revision.

### 5. References

- **[E] Submission-stage flexibility:** CRST imposes no strict reference-format requirement at initial submission, provided one style is used consistently and complete bibliographic data are supplied. The journal style is applied after acceptance.
- **[E] Target journal style:** In-text citations are author–year: one author `(Author, year)`, two authors `(Author and Author, year)`, and three or more `(Author et al., year)`. The reference list is alphabetical, then chronological where needed; same-author/same-year works use a/b/c. Journal names are abbreviated according to LTWA.
- **[E] Integrity/completeness:** Every in-text citation must be in the reference list and vice versa; every reference must be a real source; include DOI where available.
- **[E] Data/software citations:** The Guide gives explicit dataset and software reference examples. Dataset citations should include authors, title, repository, version where available, year, persistent identifier, and `[dataset]` immediately before the reference.

### 6. Research data and code

- **[E]** CRST applies Elsevier research-data **Option C**. Authors are required to (1) deposit research data in a relevant repository and (2) cite and link the dataset in the article; if sharing is not possible, explain why.
- **[E]** A **data-availability statement is required at submission** and is published with the article. Restricted/sensitive data may be justified in the submission statement.
- **[E]** “Research data” expressly includes software, code, models, algorithms, protocols, methods, and other project materials in addition to observations/experimental results.
- **[E]** Provide the repository link when prompted in submission and use persistent identifiers in the manuscript where appropriate.
- **[I]** For a computational roof-snow study, the safest compliance package is a versioned archival release of analysis/simulation code plus the exact input and result data needed to verify findings, each with a persistent identifier, cited in the manuscript. The Guide does not prescribe GitHub, Zenodo, or a specific license.

### 7. Declarations and ethics

- **[E] Submission declaration:** Submission implies that the work is not previously published except allowed forms (e.g., preprint, abstract, lecture, thesis, registered report), is not under consideration elsewhere, is approved by all authors/responsible authorities, and will not be republished in the same form without copyright-holder consent.
- **[E] Competing interests:** All authors must disclose financial/personal relationships. The Elsevier declarations tool “should always be completed”; authors with none select “I have nothing to declare.” Upload the resulting declaration as a `.doc`/`.docx` file at the attach/upload-files step; signatures are not required.
- **[E] Funding:** Identify funders/grant numbers and state funder roles in design, data collection/analysis/interpretation, writing, and submission decision. If unfunded, Elsevier recommends: “This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.”
- **[E] Authorship:** Authors must substantially contribute to conception/design or data acquisition/analysis/interpretation, drafting or critical revision, and final approval; all are accountable. A single corresponding author must be appointed.

### 8. Generative AI

- **[E] Manuscript preparation:** AI may support preparation only with human oversight; it cannot replace critical thinking or evaluation. Authors remain responsible for accuracy, completeness, impartiality, originality, source verification, privacy, IP, and tool terms.
- **[E] Disclosure:** Disclose manuscript-preparation AI in a separate declaration at submission, naming the tool/service, purpose, and author oversight. The CRST Guide places the section before the references. Basic grammar/spelling/reference checks do not require disclosure; substantive changes to sentence structure or organization do.
- **[E] Research use:** AI used as part of research must be described reproducibly in Methods, including tool/model name, version, and developer/manufacturer where applicable.
- **[E] Authorship:** AI tools cannot be authors/co-authors and should not be cited as authors.
- **[E] Images:** AI may support explanatory images if disclosed both in the caption (tool, version, use) and general AI statement. AI-supported data visualization is allowed only when faithfully and reproducibly derived from underlying data; disclose the tool/model, version, and developer in Methods. AI must not fabricate/alter data or create/alter primary research images not directly obtained in the research.
- **[E] Graphical abstracts:** Elsevier’s current detailed policy says **general-purpose generative-AI image tools must not be used to create graphical abstracts**; dedicated scientific illustration tools are encouraged.

### 9. Submission files and online submission

- **[E]** Upload all required editable manuscript files, separate artwork, videos, supplements, tables/footnotes, and captions. Editorial Manager converts article files to one PDF for peer review, but editable files remain required for production.
- **[E]** Checklist items include designated corresponding author with current details, spell/grammar checks, bidirectional reference checking, permissions for copyrighted third-party material, and continuous line numbering.
- **[E]** The Guide does not state a mandatory reporting checklist (e.g., CONSORT/STROBE) for all CRST articles; use a study-design-specific checklist if applicable.

### 10. Cover letter

- **[E—journal-specific finding]** The current CRST Guide contains **no cover-letter section or journal-specific cover-letter content rule**.
- **[E—generic Elsevier guidance, not CRST-specific]** Elsevier nevertheless says to include a short, focused cover letter (ideally under one page) stating the study aim/main findings, fit with journal aims/scope, novelty and broader implications, and any invitation to submit. Do **not** put funding, author declarations, or reviewer suggestions/oppositions in the letter. Elsevier notes that an individual journal may require a letter and directs authors to its Guide.
- **[I]** Prepare the generic one-page Elsevier letter, but treat mandatory upload status as unverified until the live CRST Editorial Manager submission workflow displays its file requirements.

## Verification table

| Official source | Identifier / DOI | Claim supported | Verification URL | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | Aims/scope; article types; review model | https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/cold-regions-science-and-technology/publish/guide-for-authors | High |
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | Editable `.doc/.docx`/`.tex`; PDF not source; title page; abstract ≤250 words; 1–7 keywords | Same URL | High |
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | Mandatory separate highlights: 3–5 bullets, ≤85 characters each; continuous line numbers | Same URL | High |
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | Editable tables; separate figure files; formats and 300/1000-dpi thresholds | Same URL | High |
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | Consistent references accepted at submission; author–year/alphabetical target style; dataset/software citation | Same URL | High |
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | Option C data deposit/citation/linking; required data statement; research data includes code/software/models | Same URL | High |
| CRST Guide for authors | Journal ISSN 0165-232X; page DOI: none | COI `.doc/.docx`; funding disclosure; AI declaration; CRediT | Same URL | High |
| Generative AI policies for journals | Page DOI: none | AI disclosure, human accountability, Methods reporting, image/data-visualization controls, ban on general-purpose GenAI for graphical abstracts | https://www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/generative-ai-policies-for-journals | High |
| Elsevier Support: cover letter | Page DOI: none; updated 18 May 2026 | Generic letter content and exclusions; journal-specific requirements must come from Guide | https://www.elsevier.support/publishing/answer/what-should-be-included-in-a-cover-letter | High for generic guidance; Medium for CRST operational necessity |

## Critical gaps / items that cannot be verified from the public CRST Guide

1. Whether the live CRST Editorial Manager workflow currently marks a cover letter as required or optional.
2. Any hidden per-file size constraints or metadata-field limits imposed by Editorial Manager.
3. Article-type-specific body-word/page/figure/table/reference limits: none are published in the current Guide.
4. The editor’s project-specific judgment on whether this particular manuscript fits CRST scope.

No repository files were edited.

    critical_gaps: Public official sources do not reveal whether CRST Editorial Manager currently requires a cover letter, hidden file/field limits, or unpublished article-type length/count limits; manuscript-specific scope fit remains an editorial judgment.

    report: # Verified CRST literature: roof snow load, deposition, shedding, and control

## Scope and verification standard

This is a focused—not exhaustive—set of *Cold Regions Science and Technology* (CRST) papers with direct relevance to roof snow or clearly labeled adjacent relevance to sliding/adhesion/control. Bibliographic fields were independently matched against Crossref and Elsevier core metadata. Claims below are limited to publisher abstracts/highlights or authoritative institutional copies/summaries. **High** confidence means both metadata and the stated claim were directly supported; **Medium** is used once where the CRST metadata is direct but the methodological interpretation is triangulated through the authors’ companion paper rather than a retrievable CRST abstract.

## Evidence synthesis

- **Roof geometry and wind jointly control deposition.** Large-scale measurements found larger surrounding drifts for a flat roof than a single-pitch roof and larger drifts for an upstream-tilted than downstream-tilted single-pitch roof. Flat-roof wind-tunnel tests further located the usual maximum near the windward region, with a possible rear peak on large spans.
- **CFD is useful only with empirical validation and explicit model limits.** The CRST review identifies strong potential for roof-snow prediction but calls for validation databases, practical guidance, and continued reliance on observations. Applied studies demonstrate validated multiphase approaches and coupling of simulated nonuniform snow load to structural analysis.
- **Meteorological load models should not reduce roof snow to precipitation alone.** Wind-dominated deposition and transport can create unbalanced loads; a northern-China analysis explicitly treats joint snowfall, wind, and temperature indicators.
- **Slope and surface energy affect shedding, but adjacent evidence must not be overstated.** Monoslope experiments separate lower-slope (0–10°) from higher-slope (15–25°) drift behavior. The PV study supports snow transmittance and transmitted solar radiation as sliding/melting predictors; it is not a general roof-snow-load validation.
- **Adhesion evidence is mechanistically relevant but not roof-specific.** On metallic surfaces, liquid-water content and roughness strongly affect adhesion; wet snow showed higher shear adhesion but lower tensile adhesion than dry snow, consistent with capillary-dominated tensile behavior.
- **The verified CRST control paper is active, not passive.** The automatic membrane-roof system uses electrical heating wires and thermal control. It must not be cited as evidence for passive or functionally graded snow shedding.

## Verification table

| Verified source | Identifier / DOI | Precise claim supported | Verification URL | Confidence |

| Giever PM, Sack RL. **Similitude considerations for roof snow loads.** CRST. 1990;19(1):59–71. | `10.1016/0165-232X(90)90018-R` | Foundational support for using explicit similitude to relate laboratory model roof loads to prototype roof loads. The companion 1990 paper by the same authors states that measured laboratory gable-roof loads were transferred to prototypes through similitude; no quantitative rule from the CRST paper is asserted here. | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/0165-232X(90)90018-R) · [companion ASCE abstract](https://ascelibrary.org/doi/10.1061/%28ASCE%290733-9445%281990%29116%3A10%282763%29) | **Medium** |
| Thiis TK, Gjessing Y. **Large-scale measurements of snowdrifts around flat-roofed and single-pitch-roofed buildings.** CRST. 1999;30(1–3):175–181. | `10.1016/S0165-232X(99)00021-X` | In same-footprint models at Spitsbergen, roof design significantly changed drift size: flat roofs produced larger drifts than single-pitch roofs; upstream-tilted single-pitch roofs produced larger drifts than downstream-tilted roofs. | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-232X(99)00021-X) · [institutional full text](https://arc.lib.montana.edu/snow-science/objects/issw-1998-067-072.pdf) | **High** |
| Zhou X, Kang L, Yuan X, Gu M. **Wind tunnel test of snow redistribution on flat roofs.** CRST. 2016;127:49–56. | `10.1016/j.coldregions.2016.04.006` | Silica-sand wind-tunnel tests found the largest depth usually near the windward region, with a possible rear peak on large-span roofs; transport increased with wind velocity/span, particle-transport efficiency declined with duration, and roof-average mass flux asymptotically declined with span. | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2016.04.006) · [publisher abstract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165232X16300581) | **High** |

Heating-wire spacing/power and wind, irradiation, ambient temperature, and snow depth were evaluated using snow-free-area ratio and temperature variation. This supports active snow removal only. | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2022.103754) · [publisher abstract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165232X22002737) | **High; active control** |
| Tominaga Y, Igarashi K, Wakui M, Motoyoshi H, Ito Y. **Measurement and estimation of temporal variations of roof snow load on semi-full-scale building model.** CRST. 2025;232:104445. | `10.1016/j.coldregions.2025.104445` | Load cells, drainpipe discharge, meteorology, and ground-snow measurements provided validation data. A degree-day method estimated peak roof snow weight to about 10% accuracy when precipitation catch ratio and exposed snow-side-surface effects were treated appropriately. | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2025.104445) · [publisher article](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165232X2500028X) | **High** |
| Fasani D, Cernuschi F, Wolfsperger F, Balordi M, Colombo LPM. **Shear and tensile adhesion of dry and wet snow on metallic surfaces.** CRST. 2026;249:104971. | `10.1016/j.coldregions.2026.104971` | Controlled laboratory/field measurements show strong dependence on liquid-water content and surface roughness. Wet snow had substantially higher shear adhesion, whereas tensile adhesion was lower than dry snow and consistent with capillary-dominated adhesion. This is material-interface evidence, not roof-system validation. | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2026.104971) · [authoritative RSE summary](https://www.rse-web.it/en/news/snow-adhesion-on-metallic-surfaces-a-new-study-published-from-the-collaboration-between-rse-slf-and-politecnico-di-milano/) | **High; adjacent** |

## Critical gap for a passive/functionally graded roof claim

No paper in the verified CRST set directly tests a **passive, functionally graded roof surface** for snow shedding or load reduction. The defensible literature bridge is limited to: (1) physical roof deposition/load studies; (2) adjacent PV sliding/melting parameters; and (3) metallic-surface adhesion mechanics. The electrical–thermal membrane roof is an active-control comparator and must not be characterized as passive. A manuscript should therefore present passive functional grading as the study’s unresolved design hypothesis/contribution, not as an established CRST result.

## Reproducibility note

No repository files were edited. Raw Crossref records, Elsevier core-metadata responses, DOI landing snapshots, institutional evidence, and search snapshots were preserved under `/home/ubuntu/research/crst-literature-2026-09-24/raw/`. The machine-readable acquisition ledger records source URLs, identifiers, UTC acquisition times, conditions, storage paths, byte sizes, SHA-256 checksums, and usage notes for every raw file.

    critical_gaps: No verified CRST paper in the retained set directly tests a passive, functionally graded roof surface. The closest evidence is adjacent (PV sliding/melting and snow adhesion on metallic surfaces), while the verified membrane-roof control study is explicitly active electrical–thermal control.

    report: # Japanese snow-retention / non-shedding roof practice

## Bottom line

Japanese practice treats roof snow as a **whole-building and site-management problem**, not a single roof-product choice. The main strategies are: (1) retain snow on a structurally designed roof (無落雪屋根 / non-shedding roof), (2) shed it deliberately into protected storage space, (3) restrain it on a sloped roof with guards or high-friction detailing, or (4) melt some or all of it using supplied heat. Japanese evidence does **not** support a universal roof pitch, snow-guard spacing, friction coefficient, or melting design transferable to other climates.

## Technical synthesis

| Strategy | Japanese practice and benefit | Principal limitations / failure modes |
|---|---|---|
| **無落雪屋根: M-shaped / “snow-duct” roof** | Opposing roof planes drain toward a central horizontal gutter and internal downpipe. Common where uncontrolled snow discharge would reach roads or neighboring lots. It retains snow rather than relying on routine sliding. | Retained snow load still requires local structural design. Central drains can clog; gutter joints and sealants can leak; safe performance depends on continuous insulation, air/vapor control, attic ventilation, drainage inspection, and overflow detailing. Kimura found the M-roof’s practical value was avoidance of eave ice dams/icicles—not meaningful solar melting through the snowpack. |
| **Flat or very-low-slope non-shedding roof** | Eliminates large planned slide paths and suits compact lots; snow is carried until melting, sublimation, redistribution, or removal. | “Non-shedding” does not mean hazard-free. Wind redistribution, edge drift, and overhanging snow cornices can create concentrated loads and falling-snow hazards. Drainage and waterproofing remain critical. |
| **Non-sliding sloped roof** | Uses snow guards, standing seams, rough/high-retention roofing, or combinations to keep snow on a familiar pitched form. | Performance changes with snow water content, interface temperature, roof slope, snow depth, product strength, spacing, attachment/substrate capacity, and aging. Partial release can be more hazardous than predictable retention or shedding. |
| **Conventional natural-shedding roof (落雪式)** | Simple geometry, sufficient slope, and smooth roofing encourage snow to leave within days, reducing long-duration roof load and some waterproofing demands. No operating energy is required. | Requires a permanent on-site runout and storage zone, exclusion from entrances/walkways, and protection of roads and neighboring property. Complex roof forms, penetrations, thermal nonuniformity, refreezing, and material aging make release timing and trajectory uncertain. |
| **Active melting (融雪式)** | Electric, hydronic, warm-air, heat-pipe, solar, geothermal, waste-heat, or boiler-assisted systems can reduce snow where shedding space is unavailable. A Nagano study found solar/geothermal systems technically viable in its test context and found partial melting more energy- and construction-efficient than complete melting. | Capital cost, energy use, controls, maintenance, equipment life/replacement, drainage capacity, and refreezing/icicle risk. The Nagano results are climate- and system-specific, not proof of universal feasibility. |
| **Load-resisting roof (耐雪式)** | Strengthens the building to carry locally specified snow without depending on shedding or melting. | Higher structural cost; retained load, drifting, cornices, drainage, and exceptional-event/inspection planning remain. It is not synonymous with an M-shaped roof, although both may retain snow. |

### 1. 無落雪屋根 is a family, not one construction

Hokkaido guidance identifies the M-shaped roof as a prevalent form and also discusses low-slope/flat and non-sliding pitched solutions. The design logic is especially compelling on compact sites: if snow cannot remain within the property after sliding, planned retention is preferable to uncontrolled discharge. However, retention exchanges one hazard for others—sustained structural load, leakage, drainage blockage, ice formation, drift, and cornice management.

The envelope is part of the snow-control system. Hokkaido guidance specifically couples M-roof reliability to insulation, continuous vapor/air control, attic ventilation, pre-winter drain cleaning, and periodic sheet-metal/sealant inspection. Thus, “copying the shape” without the thermal, drainage, structural, and maintenance system is not faithful transfer of the Japanese practice.

### 2. Natural shedding is site-dependent, not defined by one pitch

Official regional guidance gives visibly different local rules of thumb: Hokkaido recommends at least a **5-sun pitch** for its conventional shedding context, whereas Niigata material describes approximately **3/10 or steeper**, smooth metal roofing, simple geometry, unobstructed sliding, and planned snow-storage space. This is evidence against presenting either pitch as universal. Climate, snow density/wetness, freeze–thaw regime, roof temperature, material condition, geometry, and acceptable runout all differ.

Sliding performance also evolves. Experiments show that friction and adhesion depend on roofing roughness, water repellency, and snow water content; coated-steel performance changes under ultraviolet and mechanical deterioration. A roof designed around reliable sliding therefore needs durability and maintenance assumptions, not only an initial laboratory coefficient.

### 3. Snow guards require engineering, not token installation

Takakura, Ito, and Tomabechi found that wet granular snow gave the lowest interface friction; tested snow-guard strengths differed by about twofold. In their specific experiments on 21.8–30.9° roofs, spacing below 680 mm prevented creep of a 100 mm snow layer. Those values are **experimental boundary conditions, not a prescriptive global detail**. Required guard count and layout must account for tributary snow load, local snow properties, roof pitch, conservative interface friction, guard capacity, attachment and substrate capacity, creep between rows, corrosion, and edge/entrance consequences.

Sapporo’s current administrative guidance accepts adequate setback, effectively installed guards, qualifying retention roofing, or other agreed measures, but explicitly warns that building approval does not guarantee that ice or snow will never fall. This is an appropriately performance-based interpretation.

### 4. Active melting is a comparator, not an automatic upgrade

Niigata’s technical comparison recognizes electric, hot-water, heat-pipe, and warm-air approaches and identifies installation, operating, service-life, and replacement costs. Asano and Iwai’s Iiyama experiments support solar/geothermal and solar-plus-auxiliary-boiler systems for that study setting, while favoring partial over complete melting. Generalization requires local snowfall energy balance, electricity/fuel availability, drainage/refreezing design, redundancy, controls, maintenance competence, lifecycle cost, and carbon intensity.

## What cannot be generalized globally

1. **Regional Japanese numbers:** Hokkaido’s colder/drier conditions and Hokuriku/Niigata’s warmer, wetter, denser snow produce different sliding, adhesion, load, and drainage behavior.
2. **Pitch or spacing thresholds:** The reported 5-sun and 3/10 pitches and 680 mm guard spacing are context-specific guidance or experiments, not international design values.
3. **Material behavior:** Much of the evidence concerns Japanese coated-steel roofing and specific test snow; other membranes, metals, coatings, corrosion environments, and aging histories can behave differently.
4. **Urban rationale:** Compact Japanese parcels and local liability/setback rules strengthen the case for retention; low-density sites with safe runout may rationally prefer controlled shedding.
5. **Thermal behavior:** Interior temperature, insulation/airtightness, ventilation, solar exposure, wind, rain-on-snow, and freeze–thaw frequency alter meltwater and release mechanisms.
6. **Structural regulation:** Snow load, drift, importance, load combinations, and any permitted load reduction must come from the governing jurisdiction; “non-shedding” is not a structural-load exemption.
7. **Operations:** Japanese guidance assumes inspection and maintenance. The same geometry may be unsafe where drains, guards, coatings, and exclusion zones will not be maintained.

## CRST-relevant conclusion

Japanese practice supports a **functional continuum**—retain, restrain, shed, melt, or structurally carry—selected with the site, envelope, drainage, structure, and operations as one system. It is defensible as precedent for controlled retention, but not as evidence that one Japanese roof geometry or component detail will work globally. A globally framed design should specify performance objectives (allowable movement, retained load, drainage, protected zones, inspection state, and failure mode) and calibrate them with local snow climate and code.

    report: # JMA weather observations for reproducible roof-snow simulation

## Bottom line

Use JMA's **Past Weather Data Download** as the primary official bulk route:
<https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/>. It openly exports hourly (`aggrgPeriod=9`) and daily (`aggrgPeriod=1`) CSV for multiple stations, elements, and periods, including per-value quality information and observation-environment discontinuity information. Use JMA's **Historical Weather Data Search** pages (<https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/>) for human-readable spot checks and direct verification URLs.

The web tool internally submits POST requests to `/risk/obsdl/show/table`; a test request reproduced both hourly and multi-station daily CSV. This is a reproducible interface, but JMA does **not** document it as a stable, versioned public API. For publication-grade reproducibility, retain the original CSV bytes, the complete POST parameters, retrieval UTC time, response headers, SHA-256, the downloaded client JavaScript version, and the applicable terms. Do not build an unattended high-rate crawler around an undocumented interface.

## Reproducible routes

### 1. Preferred bulk CSV route

The JMA client currently uses:

```text
POST https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/top/station   pd=<prefecture-area code>
POST https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/top/element  aggrgPeriod=9|1
POST https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/show/table
```

Core `show/table` fields observed in the official client and verified by retrieval:

```text
stationNumList   JSON array, e.g. ["s47433","s47575","a1079","a0543"]
aggrgPeriod      9 hourly; 1 daily
elementNumList   JSON array, e.g. [["201",""],["101",""],["503",""],["501",""]]
interAnnualType  1 for a continuous period
ymdList          [startYear,endYear,startMonth,endMonth,startDay,endDay]
optionNumList    JSON array; [] if no normals/comparison columns
downloadFlag     true
rmkFlag          1 to retain values requiring attention and their quality columns
disconnectFlag   1 to retain all periods and homogeneity-number columns
csvFlag          1 for numeric CSV
jikantaiFlag     0 for all 24 hours
jikantaiList     ["1","24"]
ymdLiteral       1 for date-time literals
```

The downloaded file is CP932/Shift_JIS despite an `application/octet-stream` response; preserve the original and make a separate UTF-8 derivative. The tool enforces a workload meter, so retrieve large studies in deterministic station/winter chunks and record every chunk. A four-station daily request and a 24-hour Sukayu request were successfully reproduced with these parameters.

### 2. Readable audit URLs

```text
Hourly observatory:
https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/hourly_s1.php?prec_no=PP&block_no=BBBBB&year=YYYY&month=MM&day=DD&view=p1

Hourly AMeDAS:
https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/hourly_a1.php?prec_no=PP&block_no=BBBB&year=YYYY&month=MM&day=DD&view=p1

Daily observatory:
https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/daily_s1.php?prec_no=PP&block_no=BBBBB&year=YYYY&month=MM&day=&view=p1

Daily AMeDAS:
https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/daily_a1.php?prec_no=PP&block_no=BBBB&year=YYYY&month=MM&day=&view=p1
```

Example: Sukayu hourly, 15 January 2024:
<https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/hourly_a1.php?prec_no=31&block_no=1079&year=2024&month=01&day=15&view=p1>.

## Neutral candidate station panel

`s` denotes a JMA observatory/synoptic station in the download tool; `a` denotes AMeDAS. Snow normals below are JMA 1991–2020 annual normals and establish that these are genuinely snow-rich sites; they are not simulated values.

| Contrast | Station | Download ID / `block_no` | `prec_no` | Coordinates; elevation | Annual snowfall / maximum snow depth normal |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| Cold Hokkaido inland | Kutchan (倶知安) | `s47433` / `47433` | `16` | 42°54.0′N, 140°45.4′E; 176.1 m | 921 cm / 183 cm |
| Low-elevation maritime northern Honshu | Aomori (青森) | `s47575` / `47575` | `31` | 40°49.3′N, 140°46.1′E; 2.8 m | 567 cm / 101 cm |
| Inland Tohoku basin | Shinjo (新庄) | `s47520` / `47520` | `35` | 38°45.4′N, 140°18.7′E; 105.1 m | 637 cm / 128 cm |
| Warmer Japan-Sea lowland | Takada (高田) | `s47612` / `47612` | `54` | 37°06.4′N, 138°14.8′E; 12.9 m | 413 cm / 96 cm |
| High mountain stress case | Sukayu (酸ケ湯) | `a1079` / `1079` | `31` | 40°39.0′N, 140°51.0′E; 890 m | 1,706 cm / annual value not published |
| Very snowy Niigata upland | Tsunan (津南) | `a0543` / `0543` | `54` | 36°59.8′N, 138°41.0′E; 452 m | 1,301 cm / 271 cm |

For a model needing humidity and pressure, use the four `s` stations as the primary panel, then add Sukayu/Tsunan as stress tests only after documenting their element availability. The verified daily sample showed no humidity or global-radiation observation at Sukayu or Tsunan for the test day; missing forcings must not be invented. Global radiation is also not uniformly available at observatories, so construct a station-by-element-by-period availability matrix before freezing the panel.

## Variables, identifiers, and units

| Resolution | Element ID | JMA quantity | Unit / interpretation |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Hourly | `201` | Air temperature | °C |
| Hourly | `101` | Precipitation | mm accumulated over the preceding hour; gauge precipitation is melted liquid-water equivalent |
| Hourly | `503` | Snowfall depth | cm over the preceding hour; JMA derives snowfall depth from changes in measured snow depth |
| Hourly | `501` | Snow depth | cm, ground snow depth |
| Hourly | `301` | Wind speed and direction | m/s and 16-point direction; speed/direction represent the preceding 10-minute mean |
| Hourly | `401` | Sunshine duration | h over the preceding hour |
| Hourly | `610` | Global solar radiation | MJ/m² over the preceding hour where available |
| Hourly | `601`, `602` | Station / sea-level pressure | hPa |
| Hourly | `604`, `605`, `612` | Vapor pressure / relative humidity / dew point | hPa / % / °C |
| Daily | `201`, `202`, `203` | Mean / maximum / minimum temperature | °C |
| Daily | `101`, `105` with subparameter `1` | Total / maximum one-hour precipitation | mm |
| Daily | `501`, `503` | Maximum snow depth / total snowfall | cm |
| Daily | `301`, `302` | Mean / maximum wind | m/s, with direction fields where supplied |
| Daily | `401`, `610` | Sunshine / total global radiation | h / MJ/m² |
| Daily | `601`, `602`, `604`, `605`, `606` | Pressure, vapor pressure, mean/minimum humidity | hPa / % |

JMA AMeDAS nominal reporting resolution is 0.1 °C, 0.5 mm precipitation, 0.1 m/s wind, 0.1 h sunshine, 1 cm snow depth, and 1% relative humidity. Availability varies by station and era. For non-observatory AMeDAS sites, sunshine after **2 March 2021** is an estimate from JMA's gridded estimated meteorological distribution rather than the earlier on-site sunshine measurement.

## Quality, missingness, and discontinuities

Select numeric CSV and retain quality and homogeneity columns.

| Quality code | JMA meaning | Recommended treatment |
|---:|---|---|
| `8` | Normal; no source-data loss | Accept |
| `5` | Quasi-normal; missing source material remains within the allowed range, generally about 80% completeness | Accept only under a preregistered rule; sensitivity-test |
| `4` | Insufficient source material | Exclude from primary analysis or flag explicitly |
| `2` | Very doubtful value; hourly only | Exclude pending manual verification |
| `1` | Missing statistic | Keep null; never zero-fill |
| `0` | Not an observed/statistical item, including some reference normals | Structurally unavailable; do not impute as an observation |

The detailed Help 3 table gives the mapping above. Help 1 contains an apparent contradictory sentence stating that numeric-CSV missingness receives quality `0`; this conflicts with Help 3's explicit table (`1` missing, `0` non-item). A production parser should preserve the raw code, distinguish `0` from `1`, and include fixtures covering both before analysis.

For observatory precipitation, sunshine, or snowfall, numeric CSV can also include **phenomenon-none information** (`1` no phenomenon, `0` phenomenon occurred). Do not conflate this with missingness. Homogeneity numbers identify observation-environment regimes: values with different numbers are not simply comparable. Numbers are assigned afresh, oldest first, for each CSV retrieval, so do not join separately downloaded chunks by the number alone; retain full overlapping extraction context and align boundaries by timestamp/metadata.

## Required transformations for snow simulation

1. **Preserve provenance:** archive original bytes; store request parameters, UTC retrieval time, SHA-256, terms URL, and a separate UTF-8 derivative.
2. **Parse multirow headers:** station, variable, phenomenon-none, quality, and homogeneity are separate logical fields.
3. **Time:** label source time as JST (`Asia/Tokyo`, UTC+09:00; no daylight saving). Bulk CSV already emitted the final hourly record as next-day `00:00`; the HTML hourly view may label it `24`, which must be rolled to the following date before conversion to UTC.
4. **Intervals:** precipitation, snowfall, sunshine, and hourly radiation are preceding-hour accumulations; temperature/snow depth are state observations. Do not shift all columns identically.
5. **Snow quantities:** precipitation is liquid-water equivalent in mm; snowfall and snow depth are geometric cm. Converting either to snow mass or roof load requires an explicit, validated density/compaction/phase model. Ground snow depth is not roof snow depth and does not represent wind redistribution, sliding, or roof heat loss.
6. **Wind:** preserve the 16-point direction and calm/missing categories; if converting to degrees, document the lookup and circular treatment.
7. **Quality:** propagate all flags through resampling. Never convert blanks, `///`, quality `0`, or quality `1` to zero. Aggregate only under a declared completeness rule.
8. **Discontinuities:** do not compare across homogeneity regimes without adjustment or a regime indicator.
9. **Availability changes:** freeze a station-element-period matrix before simulation. Treat the 2021 AMeDAS sunshine-method change as a measurement-regime change.

## Scientifically neutral station and winter selection

Predeclare the algorithm before viewing simulation outcomes.

1. **Station strata:** choose at least one site from each prespecified contrast—cold Hokkaido inland, low-elevation maritime, inland basin, warmer Japan-Sea lowland—and optionally mountain/upland stress sites. Select within strata by required-variable coverage and record length, not by simulated roof load.
2. **Eligibility:** require the same core hourly variables for the entire fixed snow season (for example, 1 November–30 April), a stable or explicitly modelled homogeneity regime, and a preregistered completeness threshold. A defensible starting rule is at least 95% quality `8`/`5` values for every core forcing, with sensitivity analyses at stricter/looser thresholds and no missingness during selected peak events.
3. **Common period:** use the largest common set of eligible winters across the fixed station panel. Label a winter by its starting year and never mix calendar-year snow statistics with cross-year simulation seasons.
4. **Winter severity:** rank winters using observed JMA quantities fixed in advance—preferably station-specific percentile of seasonal maximum snow depth or cumulative snowfall. Station-relative percentiles avoid favoring intrinsically snowier climates.
5. **Contrasting winters:** if all eligible winters cannot be simulated, select deterministically nearest to prespecified percentiles (for example 50th, 85th, and 95th) with a fixed tie-break such as earliest winter. For wet-snow contrast, add mean winter temperature or rain-on-snow hours as a second prespecified axis and use a deterministic maximin selection.
6. **No outcome selection:** do not choose stations or winters because they maximize the proposed model's load, failure, or treatment effect. Report excluded seasons and repeat the primary conclusion over all eligible winters or with leave-one-winter/station-out sensitivity analysis.

## Terms

JMA states that content without a separate rights notice may be used under the **Public Data Use Terms, Version 1.0**. Cite the JMA page and URL; if data are decoded, merged, filtered, converted to UTC, or otherwise transformed, explicitly state that processing was performed and do not imply that JMA created the derivative. No DOI was shown on the official product pages inspected; cite the official product, station identifiers, exact URL/request, and retrieval date rather than inventing a DOI.

## Verification table

| Source | Identifier / DOI | Claim supported | Verification URL | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| JMA Past Weather Data Download | No DOI shown; official JMA web product | Open multi-station, multi-element, multi-period CSV route | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/> | High |

| JMA download Help 3 | No DOI shown; `obsdl/help3` | CSV structure, quality codes, phenomenon-none and homogeneity semantics | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/top/help3> | High for the explicit table; exact missing-code documentation has an internal Help 1 conflict |
| Official download client JavaScript | No DOI shown; `top.2.1.js` | POST endpoints and parameter names used by the UI | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/web/js/top.2.1.js> | High for current observed behavior; Medium for future stability |
| JMA station selector | Download IDs `s47433`, `s47575`, `s47520`, `s47612`, `a1079`, `a0543`; no DOI shown | Download-tool identifiers, coordinates, elevations, and station type; POST with `pd=16,31,35,54` | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/risk/obsdl/top/station> | High for current metadata; request body must be recorded |
| JMA AMeDAS explanation | No DOI shown; official JMA explanatory page | Units, precipitation/wind/snow meanings, 2021 sunshine-method change | <https://www.jma.go.jp/jma/kishou/know/amedas/kaisetsu.html> | High |
| JMA historical search, Kutchan normal | `prec_no=16`, `block_no=47433`; no DOI shown | Station identifier; 1991–2020 snowfall and maximum-depth normals | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/nml_sfc_ym.php?prec_no=16&block_no=47433&year=&month=&day=&view=> | High |
| JMA historical search, Aomori normal | `prec_no=31`, `block_no=47575`; no DOI shown | Station identifier; 1991–2020 snowfall and maximum-depth normals | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/nml_sfc_ym.php?prec_no=31&block_no=47575&year=&month=&day=&view=> | High |
| JMA historical search, Shinjo normal | `prec_no=35`, `block_no=47520`; no DOI shown | Station identifier; 1991–2020 snowfall and maximum-depth normals | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/nml_sfc_ym.php?prec_no=35&block_no=47520&year=&month=&day=&view=> | High |
| JMA historical search, Takada normal | `prec_no=54`, `block_no=47612`; no DOI shown | Station identifier; 1991–2020 snowfall and maximum-depth normals | <https://www.data.jma.go.jp/stats/etrn/view/nml_sfc_ym.php?prec_no=54&block_no=47612&year=&month=&day=&view=> | High |
